## Enabling one extension must not change another's block opener

The parser offers each attached extension a turn at opening a block, in attach
order, and stops at the first one that returns a node. So an extension that
returns the parent container when it has decided NOT to open anything takes
every later extension's turn away, and enabling it changes the parse of input
that has nothing to do with it.

Both examples below enable `table` beside an extension whose block opener the
input actually needs, and both must parse exactly as they do with `table` off:

```
text            with formula alone      Paragraph
$$                                      FormulaBlock literal="x"
x
$$

text            with directive alone    Paragraph
:::note                                 DirectiveBlock > Paragraph "body"
body
:::
```

No other fixture in this repository co-enables two extensions, which is why
this file exists: most of the corpus enables nothing at all, and the rest
enables one family at a time.

**The two examples above went vacuous at 0a.11, as 0a.5 predicted.** A fixture
cannot choose the order extensions are attached in -- it names an option set,
and the facade attaches what is enabled in a fixed order, which now puts
`table` LAST. Both pass whether or not an extension declines correctly:
measured, reverting one of `try_opening_table_header`'s six declines leaves
them 2/2. **The property they were written for is now held only by
`extension_decline_yields_turn` in `packages/markdown-core/tests/api/main.c`**,
which attaches `table` and then `directive` itself and so keeps failing under
any order -- measured again at 0a.11, and it does. Do not conclude from these
two staying green that the decline is still checked here; it is not.

## An open table must not swallow another extension's block opener

The two below are the ones the attach order decides, and they are not vacuous.
D8 answers the case where a decline steals a later extension's turn; it says
nothing about the case where table's row matcher *succeeds*, because inside an
open table every line is a candidate row. Only the order answers that, and the
answer is Q9: `table` attaches LAST, so every narrower claim is offered the
line first.

Measured over 2,744 ordered triples of 14 significant lines, with D8 already
fixed: the two former product orders -- CLI `directive` first, facade
`directive` last -- still disagreed on 4, and the shape of every one of them is
this one. Under the old facade order both examples below parse as table rows:
the fence becomes `Text "::"` plus an inline `Directive` in an autocompleted
two-cell row, and the formula block becomes three rows of one cell.

```````````````````````````````` example formula table
text
$$
x
$$
.
Document scope=1:1..4:2 children=2
├── Paragraph scope=1:1..1:4 children=1
│   └── Text scope=1:1..1:4 literal="text" children=0
└── FormulaBlock scope=2:1..4:2 literal="x" children=0
````````````````````````````````

```````````````````````````````` example directive table
text
:::note
body
:::
.
Document scope=1:1..4:3 children=2
├── Paragraph scope=1:1..1:4 children=1
│   └── Text scope=1:1..1:4 literal="text" children=0
└── DirectiveBlock scope=2:1..4:3 name="note" attributes=null children=1
    └── Paragraph scope=3:1..3:4 children=1
        └── Text scope=3:1..3:4 literal="body" children=0
````````````````````````````````

```````````````````````````````` example formula table
| a | b |
| - | - |
$$
x
$$
.
Document scope=1:1..5:2 children=2
├── Table scope=1:1..2:9 alignments=[none,none] children=1
│   └── TableRow scope=1:1..1:9 isHeader=true children=2
│       ├── TableCell scope=1:2..1:4 children=1
│       │   └── Text scope=1:3..1:3 literal="a" children=0
│       └── TableCell scope=1:6..1:8 children=1
│           └── Text scope=1:7..1:7 literal="b" children=0
└── FormulaBlock scope=3:1..5:2 literal="x" children=0
````````````````````````````````

```````````````````````````````` example directive table
| a | b |
| - | - |
:::note
body
:::
.
Document scope=1:1..5:3 children=2
├── Table scope=1:1..2:9 alignments=[none,none] children=1
│   └── TableRow scope=1:1..1:9 isHeader=true children=2
│       ├── TableCell scope=1:2..1:4 children=1
│       │   └── Text scope=1:3..1:3 literal="a" children=0
│       └── TableCell scope=1:6..1:8 children=1
│           └── Text scope=1:7..1:7 literal="b" children=0
└── DirectiveBlock scope=3:1..5:3 name="note" attributes=null children=1
    └── Paragraph scope=4:1..4:4 children=1
        └── Text scope=4:1..4:4 literal="body" children=0
````````````````````````````````

## A label's contents are its own, and nothing outside can reach into them

A directive label's `]` decides where the label ends. GFM's autolink literal
runs to whitespace, so with both extensions on it used to swallow that `]` and
the directive went with it: `:b[http://e.com]` was the text `:b[` followed by a
link whose destination ended in a bracket (**D36**).

Nothing in this file needs an extension to know about another one. The label is
SCANNED at the colon and its bytes are consumed there, so `autolink` is never
offered them; what it sees is the label's own buffer, parsed on its own, the
way a table cell is. The examples below are the ones that were wrong before
that, and they are kept because nothing else pins the interaction.

```````````````````````````````` example directive autolink
:b[http://e.com]
.
Document scope=1:1..1:16 children=1
└── Paragraph scope=1:1..1:16 children=1
    └── Directive scope=1:1..1:16 name="b" attributes=null children=0
        └── DirectiveLabel scope=1:3..1:16 children=1
            └── Link scope=1:4..1:15 destination="http://e.com" title=null children=1
                └── Text scope=1:4..1:15 literal="http://e.com" children=0
````````````````````````````````

```````````````````````````````` example directive autolink
:b[a http://e.com b]
.
Document scope=1:1..1:20 children=1
└── Paragraph scope=1:1..1:20 children=1
    └── Directive scope=1:1..1:20 name="b" attributes=null children=0
        └── DirectiveLabel scope=1:3..1:20 children=3
            ├── Text scope=1:4..1:5 literal="a " children=0
            ├── Link scope=1:6..1:17 destination="http://e.com" title=null children=1
            │   └── Text scope=1:6..1:17 literal="http://e.com" children=0
            └── Text scope=1:18..1:19 literal=" b" children=0
````````````````````````````````

The `www.` form goes through a second, identical scan and needs the same
answer. It does not fire straight after a `[` -- cmark-gfm asks for a space or
one of `*_~(` before it, which is why `:b[www.e.com]` is text -- so the witness
puts a space in.

```````````````````````````````` example directive autolink
:b[a www.e.com]
.
Document scope=1:1..1:15 children=1
└── Paragraph scope=1:1..1:15 children=1
    └── Directive scope=1:1..1:15 name="b" attributes=null children=0
        └── DirectiveLabel scope=1:3..1:15 children=2
            ├── Text scope=1:4..1:5 literal="a " children=0
            └── Link scope=1:6..1:14 destination="http://www.e.com" title=null children=1
                └── Text scope=1:6..1:14 literal="www.e.com" children=0
````````````````````````````````

Once the label has ended, its bracket is an ordinary URL character again --
there is no state to leak, because the label's bytes were never part of this
paragraph's scan.

```````````````````````````````` example directive autolink
:b[x] then http://e.com/a]b
.
Document scope=1:1..1:27 children=1
└── Paragraph scope=1:1..1:27 children=3
    ├── Directive scope=1:1..1:5 name="b" attributes=null children=0
    │   └── DirectiveLabel scope=1:3..1:5 children=1
    │       └── Text scope=1:4..1:4 literal="x" children=0
    ├── Text scope=1:6..1:11 literal=" then " children=0
    └── Link scope=1:12..1:27 destination="http://e.com/a]b" title=null children=1
        └── Text scope=1:12..1:27 literal="http://e.com/a]b" children=0
````````````````````````````````

Strikethrough's `~~` is a delimiter and its content is NOT its own buffer, so a
URL inside one still runs through a `~` -- which is right: a `~` that never
pairs is ordinary content, and this is the control that says the label's
behaviour comes from the label and not from some blanket rule about brackets.

```````````````````````````````` example strikethrough autolink
~~a http://e.com/x]y~~
.
Document scope=1:1..1:22 children=1
└── Paragraph scope=1:1..1:22 children=1
    └── Strikethrough scope=1:1..1:22 children=2
        ├── Text scope=1:3..1:4 literal="a " children=0
        └── Link scope=1:5..1:20 destination="http://e.com/x]y" title=null children=1
            └── Text scope=1:5..1:20 literal="http://e.com/x]y" children=0
````````````````````````````````

Outside a label the same bracket is an ordinary character of the URL, and GFM
says so. Nothing is protected when nothing is open.

```````````````````````````````` example directive autolink
see http://e.com/a]b now
.
Document scope=1:1..1:24 children=1
└── Paragraph scope=1:1..1:24 children=3
    ├── Text scope=1:1..1:4 literal="see " children=0
    ├── Link scope=1:5..1:20 destination="http://e.com/a]b" title=null children=1
    │   └── Text scope=1:5..1:20 literal="http://e.com/a]b" children=0
    └── Text scope=1:21..1:24 literal=" now" children=0
````````````````````````````````
